items.title: Here Are the 2026 National Book Awards Winners
items.summary:
The National Book Awards honor the best books published by U.S. authors in the United States. The five categories include Fiction, Nonfiction, Poetry, Translated Literature, and Young People’s Literature. Here are this year’s 2026 National Book Awards Winners:

Fiction: Paradiso 17 by Hannah Lillith Assadi 

Nonfiction: Huna : A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming by Abdelrahman ElGendy 

Poetry: Still House in the Desert: An eco-contemplation by Brenda Hilllman 

Translated Literature: Centroeuropa by Vicente Luis Mora, translated by Rahul Bery 

Young People’s Literature: The Fight of Our Lives: AIDS in America by David Levithan and Gabriel Duckels 

The National Book Awards cycle began in mid-September, where long lists of 10 titles were announced in each category ( Fiction , Nonfiction , Poetry , Translated Literature , and Young People’s Literature ). Those long lists were whittled down to finalists in early October ( Fiction , Nonfiction , Poetry , Translated Literature , Young People’s Literature ). 

Finalists each take home $1,000, while the winner in each category receives $10,000 and a bronze sculpture. The National Book Awards also honor creators for Lifetime Achievement , winners of which were announced in September. 

The National Book Awards began in 1936 by the American Booksellers Association, took a break during World War II, and then resumed under the leadership of several collaborating book industry organizations in 1950. items.title: Theodore Zeldin obituary
items.summary:
Revered historian, author and francophile with a novelistic approach to his subject

On the website the Oxford Muse, which the francophile Oxford historian Theodore Zeldin set up in 2001 to bring strangers together for mutually liberating conversations, there is a little section on dancing. “Few realise,” he wrote, “how important a part dancing has played in the history of freedom.”

During the French Revolution, 700 dance halls opened; in the 1830s, socialists liked dancing the galop because it involved changing partners; in 1968 (or thereabouts) women stopped letting men take the lead. “Dancing is like a carnival, freeing you from what you normally are,” Zeldin wrote. “Dancing together creates harmonies between people with different tastes. That is also what conversation seeks.”

items.title: The joy of reading The Power Broker with strangers at 3 AM.
items.summary:
No one is well served by listening to pedants, but I think I’ve found an exception.

This past weekend, I was a reader at The Power Broker Marathon, where 400+ volunteers took turns reading the entirety of Robert Caro’s magisterial book, in ten minute chunks, over the course of 66 hours. The event’s organizers found their readers through an open call. A startling number of my friends and family forwarded the sign up form to me. It asked, among other things, when you would be available to read. I selected “Afternoon,” “Evening,” and after a pause, “Morning” too. I’m an early riser with a young son, after all, so I didn’t foresee any issues.

A few weeks later I got my assigned time: 3:10 AM on Sunday. Technically, a morning slot. But I’m more of a fan of Robert Caro than I am of sleeping in. I confirmed.

I’m a devoted reader of Caro, and I’ve taken up the Bob beat on Lit Hub too, where I’ve covered fellow Caro-heads , his posts on Instagram , and the 50th anniversary of The Power Broker , Caro’s 1162 page book about Robert Moses and his transformative tenure as New York City Parks Commissioner, during which he built miles and acres of highways, roads, bridges, and parks, at the expense of low-income families, farmers, and other less powerful New Yorkers. It’s a great book.

So much to say, I had no trouble popping up with my 1:15 AM alarm and heading out into the cold to read. I traveled northwest across Brooklyn towards the harbor, where the marathon was 50-hours or more old, having stretched from Thursday, through Friday, Saturday, and now into Sunday. items.title: Utah Adds 45th Book to Those Banned Statewide
items.summary:
Amid a lawsuit brought by several authors earlier this year and the recent election loss of Ken Ivory , Utah state representative/architect of the state’s book banning law, Utah has added yet another book to its list of titles prohibited in all public schools. That brings the total number of books banned in Utah to 45. 

It was already the busiest year for book bans in Utah, but now, the state has officially added 26 new titles since January. That is more than half of the full list.

Sarah J. Maas’s Kingdom of Ash , the seventh book in the Throne of Glass series, was added on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. 

Utah passed one of the strictest bills related to books in public schools in 2024. House Bill 29 (HB 29) allows parents to challenge books they deem “sensitive material,” and it also outright bans books from all public schools in the state if those books have been deemed “objective sensitive material” or “pornographic” per state code in at least three public school districts or two public school districts and five charter schools statewide. The bill took effect on July 1, 2024, and it started with 13 titles .

The bill is retroactive, meaning titles that met the state’s guidelines before the bill’s start date were included on the list. Per HB 29, any time a public or charter school removes a book deemed “sensitive material,” it must notify the State Board of Education. If that book meets the removal threshold, all schools will be notified and expected to dispose of it.

Of the 45 books now prohibited in Utah public schools, 34 are written by women. The full list of banned…

items.title: Mom Is in Her Shapeshifting Era
items.summary:
The Original Mother 

The original mother brought out the toenail clippers and sat cross-legged in front of the La-Z-Boy, steadying her husband’s narrow foot with her left hand, his calloused heel wedged in her palm. His eyes were pointed at the TV. Jeopardy . “Who was it?” he asked. There had been a knock at the door a short while ago. 

“A man.”

“Huh.”

“Selling fish from a pole,” the original mother said.

Her husband dug at his jaw. “Who is Vasco . . .” he said. “Vasco da Gama!”

“Is that his name?”

Her husband’s face fell. “Huh?”

“The man,” the original mother said, suddenly finding herself curious for anything that might shed light on the stranger that had come to their door. “Does he sell fish here often? Vasco?”

“Oh, right,” her husband said, concentrating on the next clue. “Sure.” He wriggled his toes. His ankle let out a frivolous little crack.

They lapsed into silence. 

The original mother pursed her lips and tried to clip his gray toenails, but the hot ache in her old, arthritic fingers was too much to bear. 

“Ah . . . oh! What is the Law of Reflection?” her husband said. 

The original mother let her eyes go soft. Her husband’s toes grew indistinct. As she reckoned with the crude geometry of this latest defeat, another woman, her mirror image, brought out a second pair of toenail clippers, sat cross-legged before the La-Z-Boy, and steadied the husband’s other foot with her right hand. 

The original mother’s husband jerked the legrest down and grasped both women by their wrists, shaking the toenail clippers from their hands. The mothers appraised each…

items.title: Two Trans Novelists Have Broken the National Book Awards’ Glass Ceiling
items.summary:
Tonight the winners of the 77th National Book Awards will be announced. Though this will be published before we know which authors ultimately receive the grand honor, I already know that the finalists this year uniquely—and with exquisite, hard-earned artistic merit—speak to the ever-evolving state of American literature.

Two of the finalists for the National Book Award in Fiction are trans—only the second and third openly trans authors ever to be nominated in this category. At no fault of trans writers, and all fault of the societal powers that be: This simply was not possible even a decade ago. If we’re not careful, it might not be possible once again, even before the next presidential term. It’s for this reason, additional to the fact of their literary genius, that I consider myself greatly privileged to spotlight National Book Award finalists Morgan Thomas and Julián Delgado Lopera.

From untangling the increasingly hostile and anti-trans US political landscape in Thomas’s Mad Eden , to exploring Colombia’s lively queer underground scene in Lopera’s Pretend You’re Dead and I Carry You , both of these authors’ novels prove to be unprecedented in craft, and unchallengeably excellent. Over Zoom, email, and voice notes, Thomas, Lopera, and I discussed the complexity of labels in trans and neurodivergent communities, the nuances of capturing queer joy, and the difficult onus of representation for minority authors.

Jalen Giovanni Jones: So first, I’d like to congratulate you both on the many accolades that these beautiful novels brought you, particularly you both being…

items.title: Mysteries and Thrillers You Might Have Forgotten About
items.summary:
I regularly co-host a couple of different book podcasts, and it’s a fairly regular occurrence for me to say on air, “Oh you know, this one book that came out last year, I think?…” only to find out it’s at least three to five years old, if not older. This week’s “what is time” incident happened while recording the latest episode of All the Books , where I shouted out Nick Harkaway’s new release ( The Taper Man ). I shared how much I loved Harkaway’s Angelmaker , a title I was sure was just a few years old.

Reader, it came out in 2012. It now has a Vintage Contemporaries edition. Am I a vintage contemporary edition? Perhaps, but you know what else is true? That’s a damn good book.

This got me wondering about what other crime reads I hadn’t thought about in a minute, so I dusted off my old Goodreads account in search of titles from my reading past. Maybe you haven’t thought about them in a minute either, or maybe they’ll be new to you entirely. Either way, they’re worth the (re)read.

items.title: Graphic Novels to Read Based on Your Favorite Thanksgiving Dish
items.summary:
Thanksgiving is all about sharing a delicious meal with loved ones and reflecting on gratitude. But, like all good holidays, I’d argue it’s also about books. After all that cooking, eating, cleaning, and family time, you’re going to want a nice quiet moment to curl up with a book as you digest. Graphic novels and comics make for great Thanksgiving reading, as they wake up every part of your creative brain with vivid illustrations and unique storytelling, which can help cut through that post-turkey fog.

Which 2026 graphic novel should be your date to the family Thanksgiving celebration this year? The answer lies in what dish you’re most excited to eat. After all, the way to a reader’s heart is through their stomach-brain connection or something like that. I’ve paired some of this year’s best new graphic novels and comics with the most iconic Thanksgiving dishes. Load up your plate — and your bookshelf!

If You Love Turkey: 

Homer’s The Odyssey: A Graphic Novel adapted by Steve Barlow and Steve Skidmore, illustrated by Martin Bustamante 
 You appreciate a good centerpiece, a prolific classic, the dish you’ve got to have on the holiday table and the book you’ve got to have on the well-rounded bookshelf. items.title: Groundbreaking Authors in SFF and What They Did To Change the Genre Landscapes
items.summary:
It’s no secret that science fiction and fantasy (SFF) are two of my favorite genres. Like any genre, they have their luminaries. There are the authors foundational to the genres, those who changed how readers and writers think about the genres, and the modern game-changers rewriting the script today.

But boiling this list down to just 10? That was the hardest part. There are more than 10 authors who could be credited with building these genres in the early years. I could have easily kept going to 20, 30, or even 50 groundbreaking authors in SFF who have had profound effects on me and their genres.

But, fine. 10 it is. Here are 10 groundbreaking authors in SFF who really did change their genre landscapes.

The Originators 

Isaac Asimov 
 Along with Robert A. Heinlein and Arthur C. Clarke, Asimov is considered one of the Big Three of science fiction, helping usher in the so-called “Golden Age” of the genre. While I’d argue the more diverse and character-driven sci-fi of today is more golden, Asimov’s influence, particularly with the Three Laws of Robotics featured in books like I, Robot , is undeniable.

Frank Herbert 
 Before Frank Herbert’s Dune , science fiction was the land of scientists writing bits of fiction. Herbert went another way, showing a vast and sweeping galactic empire, deep political machinations, and big political messaging. Dune blended in elements of fantasy as well. It also upended the classic Hero’s Journey, instead showing how a man can fall horribly from grace after becoming the hero.

Ursula K. LeGuin 
 LeGuin’s books always began with a question.…

items.title: An Isolated Lighthouse, The Speaking Sea, and More New YA Book Releases for November 18, 2026
items.summary:
It’s weird to write a post from the past into the future when there’s a major election happening between the two. You can’t acknowledge the outcome because it’s not yet known, and waiting until after the event to draft a story can mean, potentially, not drafting at your best. So this is to say that by the time you read this YA new release roundup for the third week of November, America will have been through a major midterm election. Having now done this for several election cycles, here’s one truth: your reading life might be impacted by whatever the outcome is, for better or for worse. If you let yourself acknowledge that, it’s a whole lot easier to be gentle when you lose your reading steam and/or a whole lot easier to understand why you’re blowing through so many books right now. Either, both, or some combination of this is okay and to be expected. Our collective nervous systems are a wreck. 

What’s true is that new books came out earlier this month, and there are new books out this week. It is a quieter YA release season as publishing winds down for the year, and as a result, there’s less diversity in what’s available. That’s true both in terms of authorship and in genre. This week’s new releases aren’t entirely representative of YA as a whole, so while you poke around and add new books to your TBR for this week, the ones you’ve added from prior weeks will be there waiting, too. 

So what’s on tap?

items.title: Gjak by Dimosthenis Papamarkos review – sensational tales of wartime Greek struggle
items.summary:
Translated into English in thrilling style, these interlinked stories of ambushes and vendettas vividly evoke the bitter conflict of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war

Nine interconnected tales about the violence of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war, and the struggles of its broken soldiers to reassimilate into civilian life, Gjak is something of a sensation. Originally written in Greek and Arvanitic, a dialect spoken by a Greco-Albanian ethnic group, and featuring characters from an unspecified Arvanite village, it was a hit in Greece in 2014 and comes to the UK in an agile translation by Siân Valvis. In her fascinating introductory note, Valvis writes of her attempt to capture the “unruly, galloping force” of Dimosthenis Papamarkos’s prose. She succeeds in thrilling style.

Delivered in a demotic, gossipy voice, these are rough-hewn stories of ambushes and vendettas, of brothers in arms being “closer than kin” and of lingering, sour regret. One of the translations of the eponymous Arvanitic word “gjak” is “blood” and indeed, graphic bloodiness is inescapable. Narrators don’t shy away from descriptions of how “shrapnel sliced [them] up like a fillet – eyes, teeth, ripped off half a jaw”.

items.title: Gillian Welch on Her Favorite Record, The Legendary Stanley Brothers
items.summary:
If I could have only one Stanley Brothers album, The Legendary Stanley Brothers (Recorded Live), Volume One —the record with the yellow band at the top, which means it’s volume one—is what I would choose. In fact, if I could have only one bluegrass album, I would probably choose this one. Because it’s perfect. You know how when you see a snapshot and, years after the fact, you can’t believe how much information is in it, how much detail, and how the profound essence of a thing is conveyed in that snapshot? This record is like that perfect snapshot. It captures what could never have been captured in a studio album, the pinnacle of what the Stanley Brothers did. I don’t know what I would do if this record didn’t exist.

In some ways, this record is kind of a mysterious thing. It was out of print for many, many years—but sometimes it seems like maybe it’s back in print. There are virtually no credits on it. James Shelton, who played guitar for Ralph Stanley for many years, told me that it may have been recorded by Peter Kuykendall, who started the magazine Bluegrass Unlimited , and it might have been a show in Culpeper, Virginia. He must have had a Nagra and a microphone out in the audience, because the applause is unbelievably loud and distorted. David Rawlings, my musical partner, and I used to joke that it sounded like the audience was breaking plates between the songs, but it’s all part of the charm and the record’s undeniable perfection.

This record is like that perfect snapshot. It captures what could never have been captured in a studio album.

items.title: “The Most Terrific Liar You Ever Saw in Your Life”: Six Books with Unreliable Narrators
items.summary:
I remember learning about the concept of an unreliable narrator in my ninth grade English class. We were reading Catcher in the Rye , that ultimate coming of age novel that teachers love to use to describe an unreliable narrator, since Holden Caulfield is, famously, “the most terrific liar you ever saw in your life.” Unreliable narrators, we learned, were deceitful or delusional; there was some reason we couldn’t trust their versions of the world.  This prompted the same question for me then as it does now: well who is a reliable narrator?

We tend to believe that things are the way the storyteller says they are—but that’s because we’re hearing it from their point of view. And everyone has a point of view. Even the most omniscient, level-headed narrator sees things in their own way. Even nonfiction texts that purport objectivity are often clouded by bias. We know that history is told by the victors. And we’re living in an era where we’re inundated with fake news and AI content. The question of what it means to trust a narrator is essential. Fiction can play with that, can complicate binaries, and can help us think about things like sanity, truth, and what the self is in new ways.

My debut novel, Universe of Grace , dances with the unreliable narrator in an exploration of some of those themes. The novel is written in a very limited third person and Grace is a character with a distinctive voice and an intense subjectivity. But because the perspective is such a close third, a reader can’t be sure whether what’s happening is actually what’s happening in the world of the novel…
items.t: “The Most Terrific Liar You Ever Saw in Your Life”: Six Books with Unreliable Narrators

items.title: A Technological History of Ancient Porn
items.summary:
The preserved ruins of Pompeii and Herculaneum, entombed for millennia by the disastrous eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE, have, since excavations began in the mid-eighteenth century, been a goldmine of detail depicting day-to-day life in the Roman empire. A little too much detail, in fact. In 1819, when Francis I, heir to the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, visited the newly unearthed artifacts at what is now the National Archaeological Museum in Naples, hoping to marvel at the frescoes, paintings and sculptures that had been hidden for nearly two thousand years, he was so mortified by the explicit nature of the Roman art that he promptly ordered much of it to be hidden away again.

The future monarch’s acute embarrassment marked the inception of the Neapolitan museum’s Gabinetto Segreto—“secret room”—which would go on to hide a myriad of artworks depicting every conceivable act of lovemaking between women, men, gender-ambiguous figures and even gods (not to mention swans and goats). This evidence of the ancient Romans’ uninhibited attitude to sexual fantasy, pleasure and diversity was so at odds with the prudish Christian mores that had come to dominate Europe millennia later, the powers that be decided the public was better off shielded from it, lest they be corrupted.

The story of Pompeii…reveals how pornography has long been the battleground on which morality and power and control are contested.

The erotic paintings and sculptures hidden in the Gabinetto Segreto would, for most of the following two centuries, remain accessible only to learned men carrying either…
items.t: A Technological History of Ancient Porn

items.title: Jennifer Croft on the Efficient Intimacy of Postcards
items.summary:
In 2017, when I began to read about the history of postcards, I was surprised to find that their first core qualities, which were brevity and exposure, were actually guarantors of closeness (despite separation), emblems of intimacy, each in its own way.

*

One version of the story of the invention of the postcard goes like this: On November 13, 1865, the fifth Austro-German Postal Conference kicked off in Karlsruhe, in the Grand Duchy of Baden, which was then six years, one month, and three days away from becoming a part of the German Empire. Until that time, the Postal Union, founded in 1850, would count seventeen members, each with a postal service of their own—some of them ancient, and some of them brand-new.

The Union was key to a broader effort to simplify communications across these and other sometimes shifting, frequently contested lines. Prussian postal worker Heinrich von Stephan was one of this effort’s most ardent supporters, and that November, he arrived in Karlsruhe with an especially thrilling proposal: the open post-sheet.

It would be made of heavy cardstock, and on one side it would indicate its destination, while on the other—you could simply flip it over; it couldn’t have a seal—it would offer a miniature arena for the transmission of essential facts. Stephan stipulated, too, that the “charge for postage should be fixed as low as possible, say about 1 silver groschen, irrespective of the distance the form is conveyed.”

This new form—this new technology—would be accessible to almost anyone, and in this way, the open post-sheet would open up a whole new…
items.t: Jennifer Croft on the Efficient Intimacy of Postcards

items.title: They Tried To Plan an Ideal City. They Made Something Much Worse
items.summary:
The idea of the ideal city as a perfectly shaped structure seems, somehow, never to lose its allure. A key theme of modern architecture all through the twentieth century was a sequence of attempts to impose pure form on the supposedly disorderly city; even before Le Corbusier and Hilberseimer tried to rationalize the city in the form of their slabs in open space, there was Tony Garnier, the French architect whose 1904 project, the Cité Industrielle, envisioned a city with entirely separate and distinct quadrants for living and working, all planned with utter rigidity. The housing was to consist of identical town houses, stretched out in long, even rows. There was an administrative section but no jails or courthouses: Garnier’s faith in the ability of his design to create a community of peaceful, law-abiding, like-minded citizens was so total that he convinced himself that such things were not going to be necessary in the utopian place he had conceived.

In Italy at the beginning of the twentieth century, the architect Antonio Sant’Elia had a similar faith in the future, although in Sant’Elia’s case it was expressed in Città Nuova, a design for an ideal city inspired by the might and power of the machine, “a radical break with all known models of town planning,” as Esther da Costa Meyer wrote. Sant’Elia envisioned rows of massive buildings, their form inspired as much by science fiction as by modern ships, bridges, and skyscrapers, “an entirely new entity arising ex novo from the ground, without having to compromise with any remains of the past.”

What all these designs…
items.t: They Tried To Plan an Ideal City. They Made Something Much Worse

items.title: Five Essential Books for Understanding the History of the U.S. Supreme Court
items.summary:
Today’s Supreme Court is widely thought of as the final authority on the U.S. Constitution. But in its first 100 years, the Court played a very different role in American society. Early Americans rejected judicial supremacy; instead, they insisted that the people retained that ultimate power to say what the Constitution is and what it means. Throughout these early years, Americans actively and self-consciously participated in a wide-ranging conversation about the contours of their Constitution through popular politics. Elected officials debated constitutional issues in Congress, state legislatures, and local assemblies. Political parties made constitutional interpretation the centerpiece of their platforms and campaign strategies. Newspapers featured articles and op-eds about constitutional problems. And average Americans wrote, talked, toasted, and demonstrated about their constitutional views.

How did the Supreme Court fit into a political culture in which the people retained the final word on the Constitution? That is the question I set out to answer in my book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History . What I found was that the justices were fully integrated into the political world because the Supreme Court was designed and operated as a political institution. Members of the Court served in a political capacity by acting as judicial representatives. Nineteenth-century justices were required to “ride circuit”—meaning they served concurrently as judges in the nation’s circuit courts, creating a balance of regional interests when the Court met in the capital.…
items.t: Five Essential Books for Understanding the History of the U.S. Supreme Court

items.title: Love the Revolution
items.summary:
In 1948, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, then twenty-nine and incarcerated in a Soviet facility—serving an eight-year sentence for having criticized Joseph Stalin in his private correspondence—began writing an autobiographical novel titled Love the Revolution. The novel, which was never completed, was published in Russia in 1999, and will come out in English for the first time next month from HarperCollins. The setting for this passage, adapted from the fourth chapter of the novel, is Durnovka village, January 1942—the first wartime winter after the Nazi invasion of the USSR. The autobiographical protagonist, Private Gleb Nerzhin—assigned to a horse-drawn convoy, but ever striving to achieve his coveted goal of joining the artillery—finally sees his fate begin to change, with the arrival in his platoon of Political Commissar Petrov and Junior Lieutenant Brant. 

—Ignat Solzhenitsyn, middle son of Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn 

*

Brant’s Magnificent Night 

On the anniversary of Lenin’s death, 21 January, a quiet warm evening suffused with a moist, melancholy mist, the company’s new political commissar, Petrov, came to the platoon to give a talk on Lenin. He had flaxen-colored hair, blue eyes, a snub-nosed face, an unremarkable voice, and an equally plain way of speaking. Illuminated by the yellowish light of a kerosene lantern in one of the farm’s rooms, Petrov offered a modest narrative on Lenin, emphasizing the importance of victory in the current circumstances. After the talk, Nerzhin resolved to come up, ask about the fate of his reports, and get Petrov’s advice concerning his…
items.t: Love the Revolution

items.title: The Man Who Broke Reality by Philip Ball review – the inspirational genius of Niels Bohr
items.summary:
Scientific discoveries are explained effortlessly in this portrait of a man whose research was driven by pure passion

Niels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work.

But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Today he would probably be considered neurodivergent; he possessed a passion for physics that cast a spell on all who knew him. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood.

Continue reading...
items.t: The Man Who Broke Reality by Philip Ball review – the inspirational genius of Niels Bohr

items.title: Nafissa Thompson-Spires’ Debut Novel Satirizes the Idea That Black Men Are Invincible
items.summary:
Rumor has it that now—in our world of alternative facts, of journalists replaced by influencers, experts replaced by AI, and of news constantly deemed fake—we’ve finally, finally done away with that dastardly thing called “truth.” Hard data is tough to come by, since sensationalism’s better for algorithms. It’s difficult to tell if any given video is secretly an ad. Not even our Google searches can be trusted. They’re calling it a “post-truth society,” and here we are, left in constant skepticism over the fabric of our reality. Did we really have a White House Press Secretary between October 12th and October 16th, 2026? Is Manon of KATSEYE really on “hiatus”? Could we really “see everything”? Ugh. We can’t even trust our documentaries anymore.

Multi-award-winning, National Book Award longlisted author Nafissa Thompson-Spires knows none of this is new. Her second book and debut novel, The Four Wives and Five Deaths of Richard Milford (a current First Novel Prize finalist) is set in the all-Black town of 1920s Newville, where the town has finally, finally done away with that dastardly thing called “Richard Milford.” An infamous moonshiner, an unloyal womanizer, and just plain mean, the town will tell you—collectively—that this is good riddance. That is, except for his four wives and his beloved housekeeper Alberta. They’d surely remember him differently, right? Unless they somehow had reason to kill him . . . Wait, how many times did Rich die?

With slick wit, a wry sense of dark humor, and a hefty dose of whimsy, Thompson-Spires deconstructs the idea of truth before our…
items.t: Nafissa Thompson-Spires’ Debut Novel Satirizes the Idea That Black Men Are Invincible

items.title: Belonging by Sonia Gandhi review – India’s elder stateswoman breaks her silence
items.summary:
The Italian who became kingmaker in the world’s largest democracy charts her remarkable journey

By any measure, it is one of the most extraordinary political stories of our age: a shy Italian girl locks eyes with the scion of an Indian political family, falls instantly and steadfastly in love, “transplanting herself” as a result, suffers soul-shattering tragedies, then takes the reins of power in the world’s largest democracy. It is a life that spans the extremes of privilege and distress, and half a century of seismic national history.

No wonder publishers have been keen to secure the memoirs of the famously guarded Sonia Gandhi, soon to turn 80. Yet when the chance came, the deal with the country’s biggest publisher, Penguin Random House India, fell through at the last minute over what it termed “an impasse over a particular issue” in the text, with HarperCollins stepping into the breach. For those unfamiliar with the sensitive political context, the Nehru-Gandhi family has been in charge of India for about half the eight decades since independence – and the principal opposition to Narendra Modi’s prickly BJP regime for the past 12 years.

Continue reading...
items.t: Belonging by Sonia Gandhi review – India’s elder stateswoman breaks her silence

items.title: The Brightness by Chad Harbach review – an ambitious sequel to The Art of Fielding
items.summary:
Fifteen years on, this expansive follow-up to the campus epic explores female agency, friendship – and the messiness of early adulthood

Back in 2011, Chad Harbach’s debut The Art of Fielding was hailed as the next Great American Novel. Set on the campus of Westish, a fictional midwestern liberal arts college, and steeped in baseball, it grappled with the big, quintessentially American themes – ambition, failure, the pursuit of perfection – that have traditionally been the genre’s hallmark. Harbach himself winkingly invited the categorisation: The Art of Fielding communes directly with the spirit of Herman Melville, arguably the greatest Great American Novelist of them all. Westish College, the novel explains, has claimed Melville as its own since the discovery of a lecture he gave there in 1880: its baseball team is known as the Harpooners; and a Melville statue presides over the campus like the genius of the place.

Legend has it that Harbach laboured over The Art of Fielding for more than a decade. When it finally emerged, a feverish bidding war saw it sell for more than $650,000 (£431,000), a saga chronicled at length in Vanity Fair. Any follow-up to such a high-profile debut, let alone one 15 years in the making, was always going to be read against the original. The Brightness, set on the same campus and peopled by many of the same characters, all but demands direct comparison. Throw in the fact that Harbach’s first novel actually turns up inside its…

items.title: I Want to Have a Baby Because I Miss the Violence
items.summary:
An excerpt from Nanny Nanny by K Chiucarello 

I had a feeling this was coming when Michael began texting heavily a few days ago. On the first snow of the season, he texted to say he’d had a dream about Jenny.

You know your friend Jenny? he asked me.

Jenny, as in my best friend? I replied.

Exactly, he said.

In the dream Jenny had gotten a tattoo of a tampon on the back of her leg, right in the ditch behind the knee, which I hear is one of the most painful body parts to place something permanent. Michael thought it was funny and specific that Jenny had appeared to him in the night and that a tampon was involved.

He texted, Do you remember telling me about those, about periods and the smell of rust that hits the nose when a flood opens like that?

In high school, I had been the first to teach him all about tampons. We were in his Buick when I explained to him all the chores women must suffer through when they begin their periods. There’s ruined jeans, I told him, and heating pads, long hours of lying horizontal or moving through the world with cotton shoved into you. A string. A metallic smell, I said, crinkling my poreless face. Here, I said, leaning over to Michael from the passenger seat. Smell this. And I shoved a fake gold bracelet my mother had purchased for me into his nose.

It’s certainly a smell, he replied, reclining back into the driver’s seat.

So. Michael had this dream about Jenny getting a tampon tattoo and he texted me, coming back into my life like clockwork, like he does every season.

We never could stop speaking for good, despite both of us acting,…
items.t: I Want to Have a Baby Because I Miss the Violence

items.title: Michael by Bob Mortimer review – heartwarming quirkiness from the comedian
items.summary:
Mortimer’s off-kilter charm energises the story of a troubled teenager in 1970s Middlesbrough

In comedian Bob Mortimer’s fourth novel, Michael, when we meet him, isn’t an angel; but he’s in a place that he suspects is at least angel-adjacent. He’s dead, or close to it, having come round from an emergency heart bypass in his 52nd year only to find himself sinking into a deep pool of warm gloop with honey-coloured light flowing at him from all directions. A disembodied voice calling itself Charles has offered him a choice that is hinted at but so far unspecified. What we do know is that before he makes his choice, Michael – a rock star who had three Top 10 hits in the UK and once danced in an LA disco with Björk and Courtney Love – is invited to revisit a single year of his life. He lands, somewhat trepidatiously, on the year he turned 14.

So back down memory lane we amble, the mysterious and otherworldly frame story intruding only in brief chapters now and again, recounting our hero’s comically tetchy exchanges with Charles. Here, really, is a sweet coming-of-age story with a delicate frosting of It’s a Wonderful Life.

Continue reading...
items.t: Michael by Bob Mortimer review – heartwarming quirkiness from the comedian

items.title: The Sensualist by Gary Shteyngart review – a delectable romp through life’s pleasures
items.summary:
From martinis to capybara videos, the novelist celebrates the little things (some more expensive than others) that bring him joy

In 2024, the novelist Gary Shteyngart flew from New York to Milan in search of the perfect midnight-blue suit. There he chose fabric, before flying to Hong Kong to be fitted for four shirts, and on to Tokyo, where he was measured by master tailor Yuhei Yamamoto and master shoe­maker Yohei Fukuda. A short king (“five foot five and a half, with that ‘half’ doing a lot of work”), Shteyngart dreamed of a fit to disappear his 52-year-old moobs (“my tatas”, “my chimichangas”) and melt the heart of the toughest maitre d’ at the most in-demand restaurants.

And guess what? The world’s finest craftsmen will give you all that – though Shteyngart, who emigrated from Leningrad to the US in 1979, argues that a great suit serves a deeper need than vanity. Trying it on two days after Trump’s second election, “it was the final certificate of naturalization … I couldn’t make my adopted country fall out of love with fascism, but at least I could enjoy my new shoes.” Clothes become an advanced form of self-care.

items.title: FSG Defends ‘The Telephone’ Following Bell Foundation Complaint
items.summary: Bell’s descendants have demanded that FSG revise Gleick’s much-lauded history, published earlier this month, taking issue with the book’s assertion “that Bell obtained his invention through theft and bribery.”
